title: "The chi-squared test of independence"

The chi-squared test compares observed contingency-table counts with counts implied by independence. We continue with the complete Turkish UniMorph verb population introduced on the [Fisher page](fishers-exact-test.qmd#the-conditional-probability), now retaining four last stem-vowel classes. Recall that independence means a joint probability factorizes into its marginals, as developed in the [foundations](../foundations/independence.qmd#why-the-characterizations-are-equivalent).

We first derive the expected counts imposed by independence, then compare them with the complete resource census, and finally assess what the chi-squared reference does and does not justify for that finite population.

## Expected counts under independence

For row $i$, column $j$, and grand total $N$, the fitted independence probability is

$$
\widehat p_{ij}
=\widehat p_{i+}\widehat p_{+j},
$$

The observed row and column shares estimate the two marginals:

$$
\widehat p_{i+}=\frac{O_{i+}}{N}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\widehat p_{+j}=\frac{O_{+j}}{N}.
$$

Multiplying them and then multiplying by $N$ gives

so the expected count is

$$
E_{ij}
=N\widehat p_{ij}
=\frac{O_{i+}O_{+j}}{N}.
$$

So the expected counts are not external predictions. They are fitted from the observed margins under the restriction of independence.

Pearson's statistic aggregates standardized cell discrepancies:

$$
X^2
=\sum_i\sum_j\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}.
$$

For $r$ rows and $c$ columns, the reference distribution has

$$
\nu=(r-1)(c-1)
$$

degrees of freedom. The signed Pearson residual

$$
r_{ij}=\frac{O_{ij}-E_{ij}}{\sqrt{E_{ij}}}
$$

retains the direction that disappears after squaring.

There are $rc$ cells, but fixed row and column totals impose $r+c-1$ independent constraints. The number of freely varying cells is thus $rc-(r+c-1)=(r-1)(c-1)$. Under independent sampling and sufficiently large expected counts, the statistic is approximately [chi-squared](../random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd#definition) with this many degrees of freedom. Sparse expected cells weaken that large-sample approximation.

## The resource census

```{r}
#| label: fit-unimorph-chi-squared
library(ggplot2)

population <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-population.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
tab <- table(
  vowel_class = population$vowel_class,
  t_initial = population$t_initial
)
result <- chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)

cells <- as.data.frame(tab, responseName = "observed")
cells$expected <- as.numeric(result$expected)
cells$pearson_residual <- as.numeric(result$residuals)
cells$past_initial <- ifelse(cells$t_initial == "1", "t", "d")

cramers_v <- sqrt(
  unname(result$statistic) /
    (sum(tab) * min(nrow(tab) - 1L, ncol(tab) - 1L))
)

stopifnot(nrow(population) == 588L, min(result$expected) > 5)

data.frame(
  lexemes = sum(tab),
  chi_squared = unname(result$statistic),
  df = unname(result$parameter),
  reference_p_value = result$p.value,
  minimum_expected = min(result$expected),
  cramers_v = cramers_v
)
```

The code yields $X^2=$ `r sprintf("%.4f", unname(result$statistic))` with `r unname(result$parameter)` degrees of freedom. The minimum expected count is `r sprintf("%.3f", min(result$expected))`, so sparse expected cells are not the main approximation concern.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unimorph-chi-squared
#| fig-cap: "Observed lexeme counts (filled points) and independence-expected counts (open points)."
cells$vowel_class <- factor(
  cells$vowel_class,
  levels = c("back_unrounded", "back_rounded", "front_unrounded", "front_rounded")
)

ggplot(cells, aes(y = vowel_class)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = expected, xend = observed, yend = vowel_class),
               color = "grey65", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = expected), shape = 1, color = "#8B1A1A", size = 2.3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = observed), color = "grey25", size = 2.1) +
  facet_wrap(~past_initial, ncol = 2, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Lexeme count", y = "Last stem-vowel class") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The reference p value is `r sprintf("%.4f", result$p.value)` and Cramer's $V$ is `r sprintf("%.4f", cramers_v)`. But the 588 rows are a census of the pinned resource-defined population. A reference p value is pedagogically useful for showing the chi-squared calculation; it is not needed to learn whether these rows differ from themselves and does not create an inference to Turkish token use.

The code mirrors the equations: `chisq.test()` fits the marginal-product expected counts, stores them in `result$expected`, divides each difference by its fitted standard deviation in `result$residuals`, and sums the squared residuals to obtain `result$statistic`.

## Recap and forward link

1. Independence turns marginal probabilities into joint cell probabilities by multiplication.
2. Expected counts are estimated from observed margins.
3. Degrees of freedom count the cells left free after the margin constraints.
4. The chi-squared reference is a large-sample approximation and does not broaden the census's target population.

The next section begins with [posterior distributions](posterior-distributions.qmd#updating-a-continuous-parameter), which represent parameter uncertainty under a different inferential framework.

## Check your understanding

1. Derive one expected count from its row and column margins using `tab`.
2. Why are residuals signed while cell contributions to $X^2$ are not?
3. How are the degrees of freedom determined?
4. Why is Cramer's $V$ more interpretable here than the reference p value alone?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. For the back-rounded/*d*-initial cell, $E=(78\times388)/588=51.469$ lexemes; the same row-total times column-total over grand-total rule gives every other expected count. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. A Pearson residual retains the sign of $O_{ij}-E_{ij}$, whereas each $X^2$ contribution squares that discrepancy and is nonnegative. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. With four vowel-class rows and two ending-initial columns, $\nu=(4-1)(2-1)=3$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Cramer's $V$ describes association magnitude in the complete pinned resource, whereas the reference p value mainly reflects a model-based repeated-sampling calculation that the census does not need. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
